status: Illustrated short reviewed. The twelve-minute edition is rendering; its final frame review is pending. Article not published.
title: I asked Codex to rebuild a whiteboard film from scratch
subtitle: From a three-minute experiment to a twelve-minute explainer, with an editable studio and a record of the revisions.
author: LeoGuoLabs
paragraphs: I gave Codex a demanding brief: study the Whiteboard Explainer film in LemoLab's lemo-opuscar, then make a new film about AI and learning. It could reuse my Chatterbox speech service. The drawing engine, story, camera, sound and production workflow had to be built independently.

The reference was Einstein in Your Pocket, a 111-second film made with three colors of ink, floating markers and a whiteboard. The nib creates each line. The shadow changes when the pen lifts. As the argument develops, the camera moves across drawings that stay on the board.

The new subject was Does AI Help You Learn—or Just Finish? I asked for a three-minute edition first, with a longer version only after I had seen the finished short film. I also asked Codex to do its own revisions instead of stopping after every draft to ask for approval.

The story begins with a familiar success: the formula works and the deadline is saved. Then the answer disappears. Can you build it again? From there, the board separates four questions: performance with help, performance alone, retention and transfer.

The research needed the same care as the pictures. A mathematics experiment reported better assisted practice grades but worse subsequent unaided exam grades for an unrestricted chatbot group. A guarded tutor largely removed that penalty. A separate physics experiment found stronger immediate learning outcomes with a carefully designed tutor. Those results concern different designs and measurements. They do not justify a single verdict on all AI-assisted learning.

The first visual implementation had ordinary, revealing failures. Lettering was scaled against the wrong font metric. A reused drawing ID could retrieve the wrong cached heading. Two pieces of writing could compete for the same pen. These were easy to miss in a polished still and conspicuous when the picture moved.

The renderer treats every mark as a timed path. Each pen has one queue, and the camera and ink use the same board coordinates. Stroke events also control the felt sound. Seeking backward must reproduce the same frame, which makes a visual error easier to find and repair.

The reference was decoded in full: 2,664 frames at 24 frames per second. The final three-minute film contains 4,320 frames. Codex inspected every one through 135 consecutive paired atlases, comparing moments by visual function, and opened 19 final stills at their original 1080p resolution. The records distinguish complete atlas coverage from full-resolution inspection. The two stories differ in timing and layout; this is not a claim of pixel identity.

That process changed the film. The title needed a stronger hierarchy. A circle crossed a line of text. Two markers shared a departure path. The eraser briefly jumped between rows. A later full-resolution pass caught a study divider touching its label and A/B labels crowding document rules. Those layouts were corrected, the whole film was rebuilt, and all 4,320 final frames were reviewed again. Explicit BT.709 color conversion repaired an encoding issue separately from the visual design.

Speech had its own evidence trail. Chatterbox generated natural-speed WAVs with retained job IDs and hashes. Independent transcription flagged words that needed attention. Repairs preserved the original audio and created new source-bound requests. Captions kept the finalized source wording while using the observed speech timing. An ASR match was recorded as an ASR match; it was not relabeled as a listening review.

After seeing the first short, I asked for another layer: people and recognizable place cues. The revision draws the same learner at a laptop and at an unaided exam, puts a hand-drawn Turkish flag beside the study, and uses a thinking pose when the question becomes what work remains for the learner. These drawings use timed pen strokes, including red hatching around the flag’s white crescent and star. An early still caught a notebook crossing a body outline; its position was repaired before the full render.

The deliverable is a small studio containing the editable composition, licensed fonts, speech client, original score, sound design, renderer, source claims, review scripts and a local showcase. The frame lab lets a viewer step through the reference and the new film side by side.

I treated this as one production, with a codebase and review record that could be inspected. It provides a way to judge whether Codex can study a reference, build a coherent film and repair its own work. A single film does not establish which model is better overall.

The twelve-minute edition expands the research and gives the learner something to do. A worked equation is erased. A related problem appears. Later, another problem tests whether the method transfers. That sequence needed slower camera moves and enough empty board space for the viewer to follow the arithmetic.

The longer narration has 52 segments. Independent transcripts of several Chatterbox takes disagreed with the script. One included an unrelated sentence after the intended line. Codex kept those recordings, compared additional transcriptions, and either requested another take or rewrote the sentence without changing the claim. For example, a repeatedly unclear phrase about practiced procedures became a clearer description of the same procedures and similar problems.

A local speech run also produced a useful failure. The Apple GPU trial timed out without an accepted recording. A CPU trial using verified model files completed a 12.12-second line in 37.8 seconds, excluding startup. Six of the final 52 source recordings came from the local CPU service; the rest came from the existing remote service. That is one measured run on this machine, not a general speed comparison.

The equation scene exposed a different problem: an eraser built for a small drawing could jump across a tall solution. Codex changed the wipe to eight overlapping passes and checked the rendered motion. Pen handoffs and speech cues were reviewed too, so the answer would finish appearing when the narration reached it.

I wanted the result to remain editable after the first viewing. The studio keeps the script, source claims, drawings and speech timing together. It also keeps rejected audio and review observations, so the next revision can start from a known version instead of rebuilding the production from memory.
